prompt: In Amazon SQS, what does the visibility timeout control?
options: How long a message is retained in the queue before it is deleted
How long a message is hidden from other consumers after one consumer receives it, giving that consumer time to process and delete it
How long a consumer waits for messages on `ReceiveMessage`
How long the queue is visible in the console
optionNotes: Retention before deletion is the `MessageRetentionPeriod` attribute (up to 14 days), not the visibility timeout.
The visibility timeout is the window after a receive during which the message is hidden from other consumers so the first can finish and delete it.
How long `ReceiveMessage` waits for messages is `WaitTimeSeconds` (long polling).
Console visibility of a queue is not a configurable attribute.
explanation: After a `ReceiveMessage`, the message stays in the queue but is invisible for the visibility timeout. If the consumer fails to delete it in time, it reappears and another consumer may process it, which is why SQS consumers must be idempotent.
example:
aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url $Q --attributes VisibilityTimeout=120
# consumer loop
MSG=$(aws sqs receive-message --queue-url $Q)   # hidden for 120s
# ... process ...
aws sqs delete-message --queue-url $Q --receipt-handle "$RH"   # delete before the timeout

prompt: How does an SQS dead-letter queue (DLQ) decide when to receive a message?
options: When a message is older than the retention period
When a message has been received more times than the redrive policy's `maxReceiveCount` without being deleted
When the producer explicitly sends it to the DLQ
When the consumer returns an HTTP 500
optionNotes: Messages older than the retention period are simply deleted, not moved to a DLQ.
The redrive policy's `maxReceiveCount` is the trigger: once a message has been received that many times without being deleted, SQS moves it to the DLQ.
Producers always send to the source queue; the move to the DLQ is done by SQS itself (a producer could send directly to any queue, but that is not how DLQs work).
SQS knows nothing about consumer HTTP status codes; only receive counts matter (Lambda event source mappings have their own failure-destination logic).
explanation: The redrive policy on the source queue names a DLQ and a `maxReceiveCount`. Each receive increments the receive count; once it exceeds the threshold SQS moves the message to the DLQ so poison messages stop blocking consumers. Alert on DLQ depth and use redrive to move messages back after a fix.
example:
# after 5 failed receives, move the message to jobs-dlq
aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url $JOBS_URL --attributes \
  '{"RedrivePolicy":"{\"deadLetterTargetArn\":\"arn:aws:sqs:ap-southeast-1:123456789012:jobs-dlq\",\"maxReceiveCount\":\"5\"}"}'
# alarm on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible of jobs-dlq > 0

prompt: What is the main difference between an SQS standard queue and a FIFO queue?
options: Standard queues offer at-least-once delivery with best-effort ordering and nearly unlimited throughput; FIFO queues guarantee exactly-once processing and strict ordering per message group at lower throughput
FIFO queues are cheaper but can lose messages
Standard queues guarantee ordering; FIFO queues do not
FIFO queues can only be consumed by Lambda
optionNotes: Standard queues trade strict order and exactly-once for effectively unlimited throughput, while FIFO queues add `MessageGroupId` ordering and deduplication at a per-second quota; this is the real distinction.
FIFO queues are slightly more expensive per request and do not lose messages; both queue types are durable.
It is the reverse: FIFO queues guarantee ordering and standard queues offer only best-effort ordering.
FIFO queues can be consumed by any SQS client, including EC2, ECS and Lambda.
explanation: Standard queues may deliver duplicates and out of order, so consumers must be idempotent. FIFO queues deduplicate within a 5-minute window (via deduplication id) and preserve order within a `MessageGroupId`, at a throughput cap unless high-throughput mode is enabled.
example:
# FIFO: order preserved per group, duplicates dropped for 5 minutes
aws sqs send-message --queue-url .../payments.fifo \
  --message-body '{"orderId":42,"amount":19.99}' \
  --message-group-id order-42 --message-deduplication-id charge-42-attempt1
# Standard: same call without group/dedup ids; consumer must be idempotent

prompt: Enabling SQS long polling (a `WaitTimeSeconds` greater than zero) reduces empty responses and cost compared with short polling.
explanation: With long polling, `ReceiveMessage` waits up to 20 seconds for a message to arrive instead of returning immediately, cutting the number of empty API calls and the chance of missing messages that are only on some SQS servers.
example:
# queue-wide default
aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url $Q --attributes ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds=20
# or per call
aws sqs receive-message --queue-url $Q --wait-time-seconds 20 --max-number-of-messages 10

prompt: You need one event to be delivered to several independent consumers (for example billing, analytics and email). Which pattern fits best on AWS, and what is the Google Cloud equivalent?
options: A single SQS queue read by all consumers; Cloud Tasks on GCP
SNS topic fan-out to one SQS queue per consumer (or EventBridge rules); Google Cloud Pub/Sub topic with one subscription per consumer
Kinesis Data Streams only; Cloud SQL on GCP
Direct HTTP calls from the producer to each consumer
optionNotes: One queue delivers each message to a single consumer, so billing, analytics and email would compete for messages; Cloud Tasks is a task-dispatch service, not a fan-out equivalent.
An SNS topic (or EventBridge rules) pushes a copy of each event into a queue per consumer, and a Pub/Sub topic with one subscription per consumer is the direct Google Cloud analogue.
Kinesis is a streaming service that can support multiple consumers but is heavier than needed here, and Cloud SQL is a relational database, not a messaging equivalent.
Direct HTTP calls couple the producer to every consumer and lose buffering and retries, which is what messaging is meant to remove.
explanation: A queue delivers each message to one consumer, so multiple services reading one SQS queue would compete. Fan-out uses a topic: SNS pushes a copy into each subscribed queue, which buffers and retries independently. Pub/Sub combines topic and subscription in one service, with each subscription getting its own copy and ack deadline (the Pub/Sub equivalent of the SQS visibility timeout).
example:
# SNS fan-out: one topic, one SQS queue per consumer
TOPIC=arn:aws:sns:ap-southeast-1:111:order-placed
aws sns subscribe --topic-arn $TOPIC --protocol sqs --notification-endpoint arn:aws:sqs:ap-southeast-1:111:billing-q
aws sns subscribe --topic-arn $TOPIC --protocol sqs --notification-endpoint arn:aws:sqs:ap-southeast-1:111:email-q
# GCP: gcloud pubsub subscriptions create billing-sub --topic order-placed

prompt: Which are common, appropriate uses of Redis (for example Amazon ElastiCache for Redis) in a backend architecture? (Select all that apply.)
options: Caching database query results or rendered responses with a TTL to cut latency and database load
Storing web session data shared across many stateless application replicas
Rate limiting and counters using atomic `INCR` with expiry
Acting as the system of record for financial transactions without any persistence
Lightweight pub/sub or streams for real-time notifications, and distributed locks with `SET NX PX`
optionNotes: Caching hot query results or rendered fragments with a TTL is the canonical Redis use, cutting p99 latency and database load.
Storing sessions in Redis lets any stateless replica serve any user, which is standard for horizontally scaled web tiers.
Atomic `INCR` plus `EXPIRE` (or `SET ... EX`) gives cheap, race-free counters and sliding-window rate limits.
Redis is in-memory and, without persistence, loses data on restart; even with AOF/RDB it should not be the sole ledger for money.
Redis Pub/Sub and Streams handle lightweight real-time messaging, and `SET key value NX PX ms` is the basis of simple distributed locks.
explanation: Redis is an in-memory data structure store: excellent as a cache, session store, rate limiter, leaderboard, lock or lightweight message bus. It is not a durable source of truth by default; even with AOF/RDB persistence you would still keep authoritative data in a database.
example:
# cache with TTL
SET user:42:profile '{"name":"Ann"}' EX 300
# rate limit: 100 requests per minute
INCR ratelimit:42:202609111203
EXPIRE ratelimit:42:202609111203 60
# distributed lock
SET lock:report-job token123 NX PX 30000

prompt: Which Redis `maxmemory-policy` is the usual choice for a pure cache where any key may be dropped when memory is full?
options: `noeviction`
`allkeys-lru`
`volatile-ttl`
`volatile-lfu`
optionNotes: `noeviction` refuses writes with an OOM error once memory is full, which protects data but makes a cache stop accepting new entries.
`allkeys-lru` evicts the least recently used key from the entire keyspace, freeing memory for fresh data, which is the standard choice for a pure cache.
`volatile-ttl` only evicts keys that carry an expiry, choosing those with the shortest TTL; keys without TTL are never evicted, so memory can still fill.
`volatile-lfu` likewise considers only keys with a TTL, using least-frequently-used ordering; it is not appropriate when any key may be dropped.
explanation: `allkeys-lru` evicts the least recently used key across the whole keyspace, which is what a cache wants. `volatile-*` policies only evict keys that have a TTL, and `noeviction` returns errors on writes when memory is full, which is safer for a datastore but wrong for a cache.
example:
# ElastiCache parameter group
aws elasticache modify-cache-parameter-group --cache-parameter-group-name redis7-cache \
  --parameter-name-values ParameterName=maxmemory-policy,ParameterValue=allkeys-lru
# self-hosted redis.conf
maxmemory 2gb
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru

prompt: What does the cache-aside (lazy loading) pattern with Redis look like?
options: The database pushes every row change into Redis synchronously
The application reads from Redis first; on a miss it reads the database, writes the result into Redis with a TTL, and returns it
Redis is placed in front of the database and proxies all SQL queries
Writes go to Redis only and are flushed to the database nightly
optionNotes: Synchronous push of every row change describes a write-through or CDC pipeline, not cache-aside, where the application populates the cache lazily on read.
In cache-aside the application checks Redis first, falls back to the database on a miss, and then writes the result into Redis with a TTL for subsequent reads.
Redis is not a SQL proxy; it stores keys and values that the application chooses to cache.
Write-behind with a nightly flush would make Redis the source of truth and risk data loss; it is not the cache-aside pattern.
explanation: Cache-aside keeps the application in control: only requested data is cached, and a TTL or explicit invalidation on write bounds staleness. Watch for cache stampedes on hot keys (use jittered TTLs or request coalescing) and for a cold cache after a Redis failover.
example:
def get_product(pid):
    cached = redis.get(f"product:{pid}")
    if cached:
        return json.loads(cached)          # cache hit
    row = db.query("SELECT * FROM products WHERE id=%s", pid)   # miss
    redis.set(f"product:{pid}", json.dumps(row), ex=300)         # populate with TTL
    return row

prompt: In ElastiCache for Redis, what does enabling cluster mode change?
options: It adds a read replica to a single shard

It partitions the keyspace across multiple shards (each with a primary and optional replicas), so the dataset and write throughput scale horizontally, and multi-key operations must stay within one hash slot
It turns on persistence to S3
It is required for any Multi-AZ failover
optionNotes: Read replicas can be added to a single shard without cluster mode; that is the cluster-mode-disabled replication group.
Cluster mode shards the 16384 hash slots across node groups so data and writes scale out, requiring cluster-aware clients and hash tags for multi-key commands.
Persistence and backups to S3 are separate features (snapshots) available in either mode.
Multi-AZ automatic failover works in cluster-mode-disabled replication groups too.
explanation: Without cluster mode a replication group is one shard: one primary for writes plus read replicas, limited by the memory of a single node. Cluster mode enabled spreads 16384 hash slots over shards; clients must be cluster-aware and use hash tags `{...}` for keys that need to live together.
example:
aws elasticache create-replication-group --replication-group-id sessions \
  --replication-group-description "sessions" --engine redis \
  --cache-node-type cache.r7g.large --num-node-groups 3 --replicas-per-node-group 1 \
  --cluster-mode enabled
# keys that must share a slot: user:{42}:cart and user:{42}:profile

prompt: How does an EC2 Auto Scaling group with a target tracking policy on average CPU at 50% behave?
options: It adds exactly one instance whenever any single instance exceeds 50% CPU
It continuously adjusts the desired capacity so the group's average CPU stays near 50%, scaling out when above and (more conservatively) in when below, using CloudWatch alarms it manages itself
It replaces instances whose CPU exceeds 50%
It only scales at the top of each hour
optionNotes: Target tracking looks at the group's aggregate metric, not individual instances, and can add several instances at once when far above target.
Like a thermostat, the policy computes the capacity needed to bring average CPU back to the target, scaling out aggressively and in conservatively, with alarms it creates and owns.
Instance replacement is driven by health checks, not by CPU thresholds.
Scaling on a fixed hourly schedule describes scheduled scaling; target tracking reacts continuously to the metric.
explanation: Target tracking works like a thermostat: you choose the metric and target, and Auto Scaling creates and manages the scale-out and scale-in alarms. Scale-in is deliberately slower to avoid flapping. Step scaling and scheduled scaling are the alternatives when you need explicit thresholds or known daily patterns.
example:
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy --auto-scaling-group-name workers \
  --policy-name cpu-50 --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-configuration '{
    "PredefinedMetricSpecification": {"PredefinedMetricType": "ASGAverageCPUUtilization"},
    "TargetValue": 50.0, "DisableScaleIn": false}'
# ASG creates two CloudWatch alarms (AlarmHigh / AlarmLow) automatically

prompt: Why do Auto Scaling groups have a health check grace period and a default instance warmup?
options: To give a new instance time to boot and pass health checks before its metrics count toward scaling decisions and before it can be replaced as unhealthy, preventing scaling on incomplete data or replacing instances that are still starting
To delay billing for new instances
To allow time for the AMI to be copied to the region
To throttle CloudWatch API calls
optionNotes: The warmup keeps a booting instance's inflated metrics out of scaling maths and the grace period stops the ASG from killing it before the app is up, preventing oscillation.
Billing starts at launch regardless; neither setting affects charges.
AMIs are already regional; no copy happens at instance launch.
Neither setting rate-limits CloudWatch; they concern instance health and metric contribution.
explanation: A fresh instance runs hot on CPU while starting and fails load balancer health checks until the app is up. The warmup excludes it from aggregate metrics, and the grace period stops ASG from terminating it as unhealthy too early. Without them a group can oscillate: scale out, see high CPU from booting nodes, scale out again.
example:
aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --health-check-type ELB --health-check-grace-period 300 \
  --default-instance-warmup 180
# new instances are excluded from CPU aggregation for 180s and
# cannot be marked unhealthy by the ELB check for 300s

prompt: You run worker instances that consume an SQS queue. Which is the recommended way to autoscale them on queue load?
options: Scale on the raw `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible` metric with a fixed threshold
Publish a custom backlog-per-instance metric (visible messages divided by running instances) and use target tracking against the acceptable backlog derived from your latency target
Scale on CPU, since queue consumers are always CPU bound
Use scheduled scaling only
optionNotes: Raw queue depth ignores how many workers already exist, so a fixed threshold keeps scaling out while a large fleet is already draining the queue, and gives no scale-in signal.
Dividing visible messages by in-service instances yields a per-instance load that target tracking can drive toward the backlog your latency SLO allows, which is the AWS-recommended pattern.
Many consumers are I/O bound waiting on downstream calls, so CPU is a poor proxy for queue pressure.
Scheduled scaling cannot react to unexpected bursts in message volume.
explanation: Queue depth alone does not account for how many workers are already draining it. Backlog per instance normalises the metric so target tracking can compute how many instances are needed: acceptable backlog = (acceptable latency) x (messages one instance processes per second). On Kubernetes, KEDA does the same for pods.
example:
# backlog per instance = visible messages / running instances
VIS=$(aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url $Q --attribute-names ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible --query Attributes.ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible --output text)
N=$(aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --auto-scaling-group-names workers --query 'length(AutoScalingGroups[0].Instances)')
aws cloudwatch put-metric-data --namespace Workers --metric-name BacklogPerInstance --value $((VIS / N))

prompt: With an Application Load Balancer in front of an Auto Scaling group, enabling the ELB health check type lets the group replace instances that the load balancer reports as unhealthy, not just instances whose EC2 status checks fail.
explanation: EC2 health checks only detect hardware or OS failure. With `HealthCheckType: ELB` the ASG also treats an instance that fails the target group's HTTP health check as unhealthy and terminates and replaces it, which catches hung application processes.
example:
aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --health-check-type ELB --health-check-grace-period 300
# target group health check the ASG now honours
aws elbv2 modify-target-group --target-group-arn <tg> --health-check-path /healthz --unhealthy-threshold-count 3
